title: After a fall
summary: Check before you lift. When in doubt, call 911.
callNow: They hit your loved one's head, or you're not sure
They passed out, even briefly, or is more confused or drowsy than usual
There's severe pain, or pain in the hip, back or neck
They can't move an arm or leg, or a limb looks out of shape
They can't get up, even with your help

steps.title: Don't lift right away
steps.text: Get down to your loved one's level. Say calmly: "I'm here. Let's not move yet."

steps.title: Check before moving
steps.text: Ask where it hurts. Look for bleeding, swelling or a limb at an odd angle. Ask if they hit your loved one's head.

steps.title: If anything on the 911 list is true
steps.text: Call 911. Don't move them. Keep them warm with a blanket and stay close until help arrives.

steps.title: If they is not hurt and wants to get up
steps.text: Bring a sturdy chair close. Let them roll to one side, get onto hands and knees, and use the chair to rise slowly while you steady them. Stop if anything hurts.

steps.title: If you can't help safely
steps.text: Don't lift them on your own. Make them comfortable on the floor and call for help.

then: Tell your loved one's doctor about the fall the same day, even if they seems fine. Mention it if they takes blood thinners.
Watch for the next 24 hours: new headache, vomiting, more sleepiness or confusion than usual means call 911.
Write down when and where it happened; add it to the doctor-visit sheet.
Look at what caused it: a rug, poor light, a step, getting up at night.
dont: Don't pull them up by the arms.
Don't give food or drink while you wait for an ambulance.

sources.name: UCLA Health, falls in older adults (cites National Institute on Aging)
